| Paper | Limitation category | Key quote or evidence-based summary |
|---|---|---|
| Burger et al. 2020; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2 | Reliability/Uptime; Throughput; Remote oversight; Calibration | GC analysis was the bottleneck; the robot was charged but idle for about 32% of the campaign. Operators received alerts for depleted consumables and failures, and most errors could be reset remotely under CCTV. The eight-day campaign included 688 experiments and 319 robot moves, but no manipulation-failure denominator was reported. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) |
| Dai et al. 2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7 | Reliability/Uptime; Integration; Cost | Connecting many modules requires each module to have a very low failure rate. The workflow required more than a year of development and debugging before stable operation. Distributed workflows are proposed, but no per-operation reliability or uptime statistic was reported. (pqac-00000008) |
| Lunt et al. 2024; DOI: 10.1039/D3SC06206F | Solid handling; Reliability; Multi-station integration | End-to-end PXRD automation is difficult because it requires powder handling and sample preparation. The response was a predefined 12-step, three-robot workflow; later assessment notes that such systems still generally need human intervention when logic changes or failures occur. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028) |
| Szymanski et al. 2023; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w | Reliability/Uptime; Recovery; Human oversight | A-Lab ran for 17 days, but manual cleaning, replenishment, and hardware-exception handling remained necessary. Human regrinding and higher-temperature treatment produced two additional targets; no arm-operation failure or intervention rate was published. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) |
| Zhou et al. 2025, LIRA; DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1 | Perception/Calibration; Error detection/recovery; Scheduling | LIRA addresses the limitation that SDL manipulation is generally open loop. Inspection reached 97.9% across two workflows, but similar colors and clutter caused errors, and recovery still used hard-coded interpretation logic. Future work includes retrying, reordering, replanning, centralized scheduling, multi-view cameras, and image-to-action models. (pqac-00000013) |
| Darvish et al. 2025, ORGANA; DOI: 10.1016/j.matt.2024.10.015 | Perception; Recovery; Scheduling; Oversight; Safety | Robust model-free perception of transparent, reflective, textureless objects remains unresolved. PDDL construction is burdensome, and joint planning and scheduling add overhead. Users favored keeping humans in the loop; half were uncertain about fully autonomous end-to-end operation. (pqac-00000006) |
| Darvish et al. 2025, MATTERIX; DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 | Recovery; Reliability; Safety; Integration | MATTERIX uses a digital twin for precondition checks, collision-free planning, and debugging, but its chemistry model is only semi-quantitative. Future work requires system-specific kinetics and quantum-chemical simulation. Gripper failures, interventions, and campaign uptime were not quantified. (pqac-00000027) |
| Jiang et al. 2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00075C | Grippers/Tools; Perception; Recovery; Throughput; Cost | Dispensing was slow and difficult for compressible, hygroscopic, or deliquescent powders; the demonstrated tools could not dispense sub-milligram quantities. Future work includes self-learning policies, visual feedback, alternative cartridges, capping and decapping, and mobile-robot transfer. (pqac-00000031) |
| Yoshikawa et al. 2023; DOI: 10.1007/s10514-023-10136-2 | Manipulation; Perception; Recovery; Safety | Reliably executing valid plans in the physical world remains challenging. Constrained task-and-motion planning addresses syntax, collisions, and spills, but does not itself provide online detection and recovery from unexpected physical failures. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) |
| Zwirnmann et al. 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2302.03644 | Grippers; Cost; Reliability | The compliant fingers cost about €3 each and handled diverse containers, but comprehensive dimensional optimization was outside scope. Future work includes scaling and miniaturization. Testing omitted some vessels, used 2 mm-accuracy displacement measurements, and could not benchmark a Petri dish. (pqac-00000036) |
| Fakhruldeen et al. 2022, ARChemist; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA46639.2022.9811996 | Integration; Scheduling; Cost; Reliability | The motivating limitation is that laboratory robots are commonly programmed for one experiment and depend on proprietary architectures or unconventional hardware. ARChemist provides reconfigurable integration, but later work still finds substantial case-specific tuning and human recovery. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000032) |
| Maffettone et al. 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2304.11120 | Grippers; Integration; Reliability; Throughput; Cost | Universal human-like grippers remain impractical. Near-term directions are 3D-printed adaptations, tool changers, vessel-specific fingers, and robot-friendly pipettes. Scaling also requires modular hardware, open software, standard interfaces, distributed orchestration, and lifecycle-cost analysis. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035) |
| Harazono et al. 2024, preprint; DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685 | Grippers; Calibration; Reliability; Cost | Commercial grippers lacked sufficient width, requiring 3D-printed fingers. Repeatability was direction dependent, and lid-placement performance deteriorated sharply beyond a 2.190 mm y-axis offset. No vision correction, autonomous recovery, or campaign uptime was reported. (pqac-00000024) |
| Seifrid et al. 2022; DOI: 10.1021/acs.accounts.2c00220 | Manipulation; Calibration; Recovery; Oversight | Human-like dexterity and hand-eye coordination remain difficult. Solid dispensing below about 20 mg may require material-specific calibration, while heterogeneous mixtures risk blockage and leaks. Proposed work includes robotic arms, continuous vision monitoring, early failure detection, and robot-friendly hardware. (pqac-00000025) |
| Sasaki et al. 2025; DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00492-w | Calibration; Recovery; Reliability; Scheduling | The system reproduces demonstrations but does not adapt when objects or equipment move; task changes can require complete reteaching. Proposed work includes vision-based localization, tactile and force sensing, compliance, positional correction, action segmentation, partial reteaching, and coordinated multi-agent workflows. (pqac-00000000) |
| Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia 2026, ADePT; DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-01932-9 | Grippers; Perception; Recovery; Reliability; Safety | Fine motor control, delicate labware, unfamiliar configurations, autonomous recovery, and real-time replanning remain unresolved. Future work calls for adaptive grippers, tactile and force feedback, richer datasets, stress testing, digital twins, standardized error and recovery reporting, and auditable command standards. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011) |


*Table: Stated manipulation-layer limitations and future-work directions from central arm-based self-driving-laboratory papers. The table highlights where quantitative reliability, recovery, and intervention reporting remains absent.*
